item.title: Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.
item.description:
Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.

Hundreds of studies have linked high heat exposure to adverse birth outcomes, but scientists are still trying to figure out just how hot is too hot. A recent study in Sydney is putting that question to the test, using a climate chamber that can reach 104°F (40°C) to determine when pregnant women can no longer safely regulate their core temperature. Finding that limit matters as heat exposure increases, particularly in places like Palau, where women and their babies face an average of 77 heat-risk days a year—and staying cool can come at a cost many families can’t afford.

Learn more at the link in bio.

Photographs by @nicholesobecki

item.title: In 2025, ski mountaineer @jimwmorrison made history as the first person to climb and ski down Mount Everest’s North Face via the so-called Super Dire...
item.description:
In 2025, ski mountaineer @jimwmorrison made history as the first person to climb and ski down Mount Everest’s North Face via the so-called Super Direct route. It was an accomplishment he’d initially hoped to achieve with his partner, ski mountaineer and National Geographic Explorer Hilaree Nelson.

Joined by his friend, award-winning filmmaker and National Geographic Explorer @jimmychin, the historic ski has been turned into a documentary, directed by Chin and @chaivasarhelyi. Ahead of the film’s premiere, Nat Geo spoke to Morrison about how he turned a lifetime of tragedy into triumph.

Learn more at the link in bio.

Photograph by Jimmy Chin

From Oscar®-winning filmmakers @chaivasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, Everest: The Other Side, only in theaters and IMAX.

Morrison takes a break at Camp II with cameramen Mark Fisher and Erich Roepke.

Photograph by Jimmy Chin

Morrison and his team climb fixed ropes up the massive, 9,000-foot North Face of Everest.

Photograph by Jimmy Chin

Mount Everest has been skied a few times before, usually via the South Col route, which is also the way most mountaineers climb the mountain. But until last year, no one had successfully descended the north face’s Super Direct, which drops 9,000 steep and icy feet from the summit to the Rongbuk Glacier below.

Map by Soren Walljasper, NG Staff. Source: VRICON.

item.description:
African dwarf crocodiles are among the smallest and least understood members of the crocodilian family. Across West and Central Africa, they are facing pressure from commercial hunting, deforestation, agriculture, and mining. Conservation ecologist and Rolex National Geographic Perpetual Planet Explorer Matt Shirley is developing new ways to study their populations and working with local hunters to explore more sustainable approaches to their harvest.

Learn more about dwarf crocodiles and the efforts to conserve them at the link in bio.

item.title: Today. Everest: The Other Side is in theaters and IMAX worldwide.
item.description:
Today. Everest: The Other Side is in theaters and IMAX worldwide.

Seven years. Three expeditions. One line on the direct north face of Everest — 9,000 feet from the summit down the Hornbein Couloir, the holy grail of ski mountaineering.

I’ve been an expedition climber for most of my life and a filmmaker for most of my career. This film required everything I’d learned from both. There was nothing in reserve.

The odds of failing were always greater than the odds of succeeding, and the team showed up anyway. Year after year, back to the empty side of the mountain, through everything that happened along the way. The camera team, the fixing team, the Sherpa team — this film is yours as much as anyone’s.

Jim, thank you for the friendship, the trust, and for letting us tell this story. Watching you dream it, commit to it, and ski it is something I’ll carry forever. @jimwmorrison

Hilaree, I hope this film makes you proud. You are always with us.

Thank you to @natgeo and @disneystudios for believing in a film that was mostly a question mark for years, and for putting it on the biggest screens in the world.

My mentor David Breashears brought Everest to IMAX in 1998. It’s an honor to follow him there. We built this to be as immersive as the mountain itself — go see it big.

We go into the mountains to recalibrate and find perspective. I hope this film does that for you.

item.title: Photo by @karthz | A polar bear and her cub share a tender moment in the “polar bear capital of the world”—Churchill, Canada—while they wait for H...
item.description:
Photo by @karthz | A polar bear and her cub share a tender moment in the “polar bear capital of the world”—Churchill, Canada—while they wait for Hudson Bay to freeze. On this day, I watched this mother and cub for some time. They took a long stroll on the snowy beach, played with each other, and had this moment that I was grateful to capture with my camera. While this is beautiful to witness, it is also a stark reminder of the impact of climate change, as the polar bears in Churchill have been spending more time fasting on land.

This photo was featured in our @natgeoyourshot #NatGeoPOY24 challenge.

A leopard patrols from a tree beneath a star-filled sky in South Africa's Timbavati Nature Reserve. Across the country, these carnivores grapple with habitat loss and fragmentation as well as illegal killing and trading. Due to the animal's solitary and secretive nature, the leopard population in South Africa varies widely, with researchers citing anywhere from 5,000 to 23,000 remaining.

item.description: Photo by @joelsartore | One of the world’s most toxic animals, the rough-skinned newt is also a survivor. These creatures have been observed crawling out of the mouths of dead frogs that had swallowed them whole just minutes earlier. This is thanks to a lethal toxin known as tetrodotoxin that is produced by glands in the newts' skin. Only one known predator is resistant to the noxious skin: the common garter snake. Photo taken @oregonzoo. To see more species featured in the Photo Ark, follow me, @joelsartore. #PhotoArk

item.title: Double-jointedness, or hypermobility, affects everyone differently, but for some, it can be more than a harmless party trick. A sign that connective t...
item.description:
Double-jointedness, or hypermobility, affects everyone differently, but for some, it can be more than a harmless party trick. A sign that connective tissue is weak, it can leave those affected vulnerable to a wide range of issues, including chronic conditions like long COVID and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

As more people open up about their experiences with hypermobility, researchers are piecing together the unexpected risks—and why viral infections may pose a particular danger. Find out more at the link in bio.

Photograph by Inge Nandrup-Bus, Getty Images

item.title: Over the summer, Vicky Ossio wasn't sure whether the 1,200 animals at her Bolivian wildlife sanctuary, Senda Verde, would survive. The sanctuary is si...
item.description:
Over the summer, Vicky Ossio wasn't sure whether the 1,200 animals at her Bolivian wildlife sanctuary, Senda Verde, would survive. The sanctuary is situated in one of the areas severely affected by anti-government road blockades that stemmed the flow of fuel and food to the region. Then came the announcement.

A recently published study co-authored by National Geographic Explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz (@paonogasca) announced the discovery of the tilcayo, the first new cat species in 100 years. Initially believed to be another cat species when it was first brought to Senda Verde by a local family, the small, spotted feline was later identified as distinct through genetic analysis.

With the help of photographers who brought the unusual feline into the spotlight, support and love poured in from across the globe, and more than $150,000 has been donated to the sanctuary, where the only known tilcayo currently resides. Nogales-Ascarrunz hopes the cat’s international profile will make it easier to find funding for the next step—more science to learn more about the tilcayo and how to protect it.

Read more at the link in bio.

Photos by @fernando.faciole

Videos by @fernando.faciole and @joelsartore, Photo Ark
